content.text:
Judging by the cognitive demands of the item itself:

- Concept depth: moderate. Students need sleep deprivation effects, the distinction between experiment and correlational or quasi-experimental designs, and confounding variables. All of this is within Unit 1.5 and 2.1 scope.
- Reasoning steps: the item is a multi-part argumentation task (claim, evidence, reasoning, a second evidence-reasoning pair). Each part is a single move, but the whole requires coordinating several. The student must also compare the strength of the sources, since Source 1 allows causal inference, Source 2 is correlational, and Source 3 is non-significant and confounded.
- Representation changes: a table plus short prose, with modest cross-referencing.
- Reading load: medium, with three short study summaries.
- Computation load: low, since students only read the values given.
- Fairness: the difficulty comes from the argumentation structure and from judging design quality. The reading is moderate and nothing is out of scope.

This matches the AP FRQ argumentation format, so it fits a full mock exam.

input.label: exam_prep
input.rationale: AP-style argumentation FRQ (claim, evidence, reasoning, second evidence and reasoning). Students must select evidence from three short studies, link it to in-scope concepts (sleep deprivation effects on attention and cognition, experimental vs correlational design, confounds, statistical significance), and use different concepts in the two reasoning parts. Each part is a single move, but coordinating the full argument and weighing source quality is a moderate load typical of a full mock. Reading is moderate, computation is minimal, and all content is within Unit 1 and 2.1 scope.

input.label: exam_prep
input.rationale: This mirrors the AP Argumentation FRQ format: the student must take a position, cite specific evidence from a table and short source summaries, and connect each piece of evidence to a different AP Psych concept (e.g., experiment vs. correlation, causation limits, sampling bias, social comparison, attribution/person perception). The concepts are in scope and the data are small and easy to read. The demand comes from multi-part structure and evidence-to-concept linking, not from heavy reading or computation. The claim is open-ended and any defensible position works, so there is no ambiguity trap. Sampling caveats are explicitly stated in the sources. That makes it a typical full-mock item, harder than basic learning but not advanced.

input.label: exam_prep
input.rationale: This is an AP Psychology FRQ-style research methods item with six parts (7 points). It covers the standard skills: identify the design (an experiment, from random assignment and a manipulated IV), operational definition, interpreting a mean difference from a table, an ethical guideline, generalizability and sampling, and linking results to the hypothesis. Each part applies one named concept to a clearly written scenario. The scenario is unambiguous and has no trick wording. The content is within the CED and needs no calculation beyond reading the table. The volume of parts and the need to cite specific evidence make it a good fit for a full mock exam, not basic learning. It is not advanced, because every part is routine for the course.

input.label: exam_prep
input.rationale: This is a standard AP Psychology FRQ-style research-methods item with six short parts. Each part uses one allowed lever: identify the design (correlational survey), give an operational definition, interpret r = -0.46, name and apply an ethical guideline, evaluate sampling and generalizability (one university, 150 of 900 volunteers), and link a table value to the hypothesis. No part needs more than one or two inferences. The reading is moderate because of the study description. The table is small and needs no calculation. The scenario is unambiguous and the concepts are all in the CED. Its multi-part structure and need to cite evidence suit a full mock exam rather than basic learning.
